vignette: Arthur Vance had been cycling along the river path, passing through a weekend market thick with chatter and movement, when his partner suddenly pulled him off his bike. He remembered the chaotic press of bodies around them, the way the noise of the crowd seemed to warp into a distant hum, and the sudden violence of her hands striking his face and shoulder as they fell onto the cobblestones. There was no warning, only the shock of impact and the realization that the person he loved was the source of his pain. His mind refused to stitch the fragments into a sequence. He could not tell a clear story of what happened even to himself. Instead, only still frames remained: the scuff of her boots on his trousers, the precise angle of the sky through the awnings, the way his own hands had hung uselessly in the air. Sometimes, the terror would strike without any picture at all, a sudden, breathless weight in his chest that felt exactly like those years ago. Over the months that followed, Arthur found himself navigating a world that no longer resembled the one he had known. His foundational beliefs about how the world works felt completely destroyed. He was certain that people were not what they seemed, that any display of warmth might conceal sudden violence. He carried a deep sense that he was inadequate, that his own judgment could not be trusted. He watched others closely for signs that they might harm him, noting the shift in a colleague's posture or the tone of a stranger's voice. At home, he would wake during the night to check whether he was safe, walking the perimeter of the house. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day. When the day passed, he tried hard to control his emotions, never allowing himself to feel or express anger. He avoided wearing similar clothes to what he had worn that day, changing his wardrobe entirely to strip away any potential reminder. These experiences existed alongside one another, a heavy, co-existing reality of alertness and restraint. Now, his daily environment as a sixty-eight-year-old psychologist had become a landscape of careful navigation. In his practice, the heavy oak door of his consultation room no longer felt like a boundary but like the walls of a cage. He scheduled his female patients for late afternoons, ensuring a colleague was always visible down the hall, and he canceled any workshop that drew a large turnout, citing administrative delays rather than his own hesitation. The clinic's waiting room, once a space of routine, now felt like a pressure chamber of overlapping voices that made his skin prickle. When he had to ride his bicycle to the community center, the familiar weight of the handlebars sent a jolt through him, and he would park two blocks away and walk the rest of the way. His wife, Margaret, noticed the distance, but Arthur could only maintain the boundaries that kept him from being cornered. For years, he had managed by staying rigid, by keeping the world at arm's length through meticulous avoidance and emotional restraint. But the quiet of his marriage had grown heavy, and the exhaustion of constant scanning had begun to outpace his capacity to compensate. He was finally seeking help not because the fear had vanished, but because the effort of surviving it had left him hollow. What frightened him most was that he would never learn to trust his own perception again, that he would spend the rest of his life bracing for a blow that had already passed. Yet, buried beneath the vigilance, there was a fragile hope that he might one day sit with a patient without waiting for the other shoe to drop, that he might remember the past without being pulled backward, and that he might, at long last, feel safe in his own body again.
